newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin faces tough choices over Kremlin battles.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin faces tough choices over Kremlin battles.

text.p: The latest battle in Russia's upper echelons of power has presented President Boris Yeltsin with stark choices and problems, the stress of which is unlikely to improve his heart condition.

Critics say Yeltsin is already a "lame duck" little more than 100 days into his second term as president, far removed from the political fray in a sanatorium as he prepares for an open heart operation expected in the middle of November.

The flare-up of a feud between Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov and security supremo Alexander Lebed poses him with a choice of whether to sack one of the generals, both of them, or risk keeping both in office and face more squabbling.

Secondly, the infighting has highlighted a split not only in the Kremlin but also in the armed forces, with airborne troop commanders siding with fellow-paratrooper Lebed against Defence Minister Igor Rodionov.
Thirdly, the row has flared at an embarrassing time with U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry in Moscow.

The added stress of the crisis may also be an extra burden on Yeltsin's health. His preparation for surgery has already been complicated by a blood problem, although doctors say they a are dealing with it.
Kulikov, ignoring an appeal by Yeltsin for an end to "verbal duels", accused Lebed on Wednesday of trying to seize power by force rather than wait for an election.

He said Lebed capitulated to Chechen separatists by signing a peace deal in exchange for a promise of help in his struggle for power from 1,500 rebel fighters whenever he needs them. Lebed dismissed the accusations and threatened to sue Kulikov.
Many commentators said the attack on Lebed was orchestrated by the political establishment opposed to the "enfant terrible" of Kremlin politics who is thought to have wide public suport.
"The crisis has been mounting for a long time but it broke out rather unexpectedly," wrote Tatyana Malkina, a political observer with the liberal Sevodnya daily newspaper.
"Either Mr Lebed managed simultaneously to annoy a critical number of Russian state officials, or the Kremlin has decided to sack him instead of allowing him to resign proudly."
The main television channels, some of them heavily under the influence of the Kremlin, targetted Lebed on Wednesday, often using comments by Yeltsin's fiercest opponents.

Kulikov is regarded by many analysts as only a weapon against Lebed, rather than the driving force. But he also has his own interests to defend against Lebed, who blames Kulikov, who rose through the internal affairs ministry's troops, for failures in the military campaign in Chechnya.
Kulikov could eventually be ousted if Yeltsin decides his accusations against Lebed are unjustified. For Lebed, the removal of a bitter rival could strengthen his hand.
Many rivals, in the Kremlin and out of it, view Lebed as the most dangerous opponent in the race to succeed Yeltsin and want the general off the political scene.
But they have to contend with the reserve paratroop general's public popularity. By ousting him, Yeltsin would risk handing the opposition a charismatic leader who might unite it.

Keeping Lebed in office would entail the risk of feuding only getting worse in the Kremlin. But to remove him would risk a collapse of the fragile peace in Chechnya, which Lebed personally negotiated.

Lebed may also be on collision course with Defence Minister Rodionov, even though he lobbied for his appointment three months ago. Russian media reports said he had called the minister's plans for reorganising airborne troops "criminal".
Lebed may also have some powerful backers with whom Yeltsin would be wary of starting a fight.
Lebed's attack on Rodionov won him the backing of paratroop commanders who control one of the army's most efficient forces.

He has also struck an alliance with Alexander Korzhakov, Yeltsin's ex-bodyguard and confidant, who has amassed huge and possibly compromising inside knowledge of Russia's political elite during his 11 years at the side of the Kremlin leader.
Financial and industrial groups could also start turning to Lebed if they decide he is likely to be the next president.
Lebed challenged Yeltsin to choose between him or Kulikov last August. The president did not take the bait, but this time it may be harder to avoid making a choice.
